# std/tls

The TLS *server* transport: listen, accept, and run the server handshake. The client
half (`TlsStream`, `fetch`) is in [`std/fetch`](fetch), and [`std/https`](https) is the
HTTP server built on this module. Importing it pulls in OpenSSL; `std/net` and
`std/http` stay free of it.

```milo
from "std/tls" import { TlsListener, TlsConn }
```

## API reference

### `TlsConn`

```milo
pub struct TlsConn
```

One accepted TLS connection. The server-side counterpart of std/fetch's TlsStream;
separate from it because the two differ where it matters — a client owns its SSL_CTX
and verifies the peer, a server's ctx belongs to the listener and is shared.

LIFETIME: `ctx` is deliberately absent. The SSL_CTX comes from the TlsListener and is
shared by every connection it accepts, so freeing it here would pull it out from under
the next accept(). The listener must outlive the connections it hands out.

#### `TlsConn.readMoreBy`

```milo
fn TlsConn.readMoreBy(self: &TlsConn, raw: &mut string, by: i64): i64
```

recvOnce that gives up at `by` (epoch ms, 0 = never), appending to `raw`: the byte
count, 0 once the peer has closed or the read failed, -1 at the deadline. That is
std/http's request-reader contract (see readMoreBy there), so a TLS client that
stalls mid-request is dropped like a plaintext one. Needs the fd nonblocking, which
acceptWithin leaves it.

#### `TlsConn.recv`

```milo
fn TlsConn.recv(self: &TlsConn): Result<string, NetError>
```

Read to EOF, as one string. For a request framed by the peer closing its write
half; an HTTP server wants recvOnce().

#### `TlsConn.recvOnce`

```milo
fn TlsConn.recvOnce(self: &TlsConn): string
```

A single SSL_read of whatever has arrived. A server must answer while the client
still holds the connection open, so a read-to-EOF loop would deadlock; this
returns after one record — the TLS analogue of one read(2) on the socket.

#### `TlsConn.send`

```milo
fn TlsConn.send(self: &TlsConn, data: &string): Result<i64, NetError>
```

Write `data` through the TLS record layer. Returns the byte count OpenSSL accepted.

#### `TlsConn.sendWithin`

```milo
fn TlsConn.sendWithin(self: &TlsConn, data: &string, ms: i64): Result<i64, NetError>
```

send that stops waiting on a peer that is not reading once `ms` has passed (0 = no
limit).

### `TlsListener`

```milo
pub struct TlsListener
```

Listening TLS socket: a TCP listener plus the server SSL_CTX holding the certificate
chain and private key. Frees the ctx and closes the fd on drop.

#### `TlsListener.accept`

```milo
fn TlsListener.accept(self: &TlsListener): Result<TlsConn, NetError>
```

Accept one connection and run the server handshake on it.

#### `TlsListener.acceptWithin`

```milo
fn TlsListener.acceptWithin(self: &TlsListener, ms: i64): Result<TlsConn, NetError>
```

accept() whose handshake must finish within `ms` of the TCP accept (0 = no limit).
Without it a client that connects and sends nothing parks the handshake forever,
and a server accepting one connection at a time (std/https) stops answering
everyone. The connection comes back nonblocking, for readMoreBy and sendWithin;
recvOnce/recv/send assume a blocking fd outside a green task, so use those on a
connection from accept().

#### `TlsListener.bind`

```milo
fn TlsListener.bind(port: u16, certPath: &string, keyPath: &string): Result<TlsListener, NetError>
```

Bind 0.0.0.0:port and serve `certPath` (PEM chain, leaf first) with `keyPath`.
Port 0 lets the OS pick — recover it with port().

#### `TlsListener.port`

```milo
fn TlsListener.port(self: &TlsListener): i32
```

The bound port — how to learn what the OS picked after bind(0).
-1 if getsockname fails, mirroring getSockPort rather than reporting a
plausible-looking port number.
